newsitem.title: ITALY: INSTANT VIEW - Italy 3-year economic plan unveiled.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Italy 3-year economic plan unveiled.

text.p: Following are analysts' reactions to the Italian government's programme of economic goals over the next three years, known as the Dpef, which was approved by the cabinet on Friday.

Gianluca Sanna, economist at Stone and Mccarthy: "There aren't any great changes in respect to what was expected. The 1998 budget will be less weighted (than expected) on the spending side but that's been done to get the approval of Communist Refoundation."
The document envisages a 1998 budget for 25 trillion lire of budget deficit-trimming measures, with 10 trillion those coming from new revenue and 15 trillion from spending cuts.
"The government has its hands tied. In order to get the document accepted by some parts of the government they are forced to remain vague," Sanna said.
He noted welfare spending would rise in proportion to economic growth in 1998 saying: "This signifies that the government intends to intervene on welfare spending."
Pio de Gregorio, economist at NatWest in Milan, said the plan came short of expectations because there were no details on how the government would reduce fundamental outlay on pensions.
"If we are entering European monetary union, then we cannot bring in the debt we already have and also the future debt created by the way the pension system works," he said.
"The DPEF was a good opportunity to strengthen Italy's fiscal position ahead of the uncertainties which lie ahead in the next few months over EMU," he added.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi said the Dpef was tailored to ensure Italy makes it to the first wave of Europe's single currency in Jaunary 1999.
Lorenzo Stanca, economist at Credito Italiano, said the document met an EU Commission request that Italy target a budget deficit to gross domestic product ratio of 2.8 percent in 1998.

"It appears a relatively credible plan but then we have to see what the budget law is like when we come to individual measures. But as a whole it is a supportive element for the markets," Stanca said. The 1998 budget law must be presented to parliament by the end of September and passed by the year end.
De Gregorio noted a comment by Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco who said increases in value added tax in the 1998 budget would only have a one-off effect on prices and would not be inflationary.
De Gregorio said however he expected the VAT tax rise to add 0.5 percent points to consumer price inflation in 1998.
The government has set itself an ambitious 1.8 percent inflation target for next year.
